title: `entire enable --force` writes the hook wrapper through a symlink, clobbering the target file and creating a self-chaining hook

verdict.rationale: Evidence shows the write-through-symlink behaviour was previously identified as a bug and fixed with atomic rename, and the later backup-exists commit says the hook path should always hold a runnable hook. Nothing shows writing through a symlink onto a self-chaining hook was chosen; the reported behaviour is an unintended gap in the version the reporter ran.

evidence.text:
hooks: never lose a hook when a backup already exists

When a hook that isn't Entire's sits at a hook path and <hook>.pre-entire
already exists (a hook manager reinstalled, the user edited it, a checkout
restored it), install wrote Entire's hook over it and the newer hook was lost.

Now the current hook becomes the backup and the previous backup is kept as
<hook>.pre-entire.<timestamp>, unless an identical older copy exists. Backups
are made by hard link (or copy where links are unsupported), never by moving
the hook away, so the hook path always holds a runnable hook and a crash at any
step leaves every version on disk. Installs and removals take a lock in the git
common dir, bounded to a second. Entire never chains to a backup that carries
its own marker, which would make the hook call itself.

Anchor a root at git's own `--git-path hooks` answer, refusing a symlink at
the directory itself; route the four hook reads through
osroot.ReadFileNoFollow; and replace the write with
jsonutil.WriteFileAtomicIn, whose rename replaces a leaf link instead of
following it. osroot.OpenFileNoFollow is deliberately not used for the
write: it rejects O_TRUNC by design, precisely to push truncating writes
onto an atomic rename.

The hooks directory needs its own anchor rather than an existing one

script is. Refusing to read through someone's link must not mean silently
discarding it, and the rename preserves the link itself as the backup.

refactor(hooks)!: remove local_dev mode

Local-dev mode pointed installed hooks at `scripts/entire-dev`, a launcher
inside the working tree that compiled and ran the checked-out source. It was
read from the *committed* `.entire/settings.json` (settings.go merged
`local_dev` from the project scope, and strategy/common.go regenerated the git
hook from it), so any repository could commit `"local_dev": true` and have
`entire enable` install hooks that execute that repository's own code. A branch
checkout could then swap what ran. This repo shipped exactly that: `local_dev:
true` was tracked, and all six committed agent configs invoked the launcher.

Hooks now always name the `entire` binary. Removed the `--local-dev` flags
(including the non-hidden one on `entire agent add`), `EnableOptions.LocalDev`,
the `localDev` parameter from `Agent.InstallHooks` across all nine agents and
the external-agent protocol, the claude-code local-dev SessionEnd timeout, and
the launcher script.

`EntireSettings.LocalDev` stays as a documented no-op: the loaders use
DisallowUnknownFields, so deleting the field would make every existing settings
file containing `local_dev` a hard parse error. It is not merged from overrides
and nothing reads it, matching the `Strategy` precedent.

Removing the feature is not enough to disarm existing installs, so this also
fixes how hooks written by older versions get replaced:

# Plan: Add Context Plumbing Throughout the CLI

## Context

`main.go` creates a cancellable context (`context.WithCancel`) and passes it to Cobra via `rootCmd.ExecuteContext(ctx)`. However, no command retrieves it via `cmd.Context()`. Seven findings, of which two are regressions the preceding commits
introduced rather than gaps they left.

The git hook directory's symlink refusal was shared by install, removal
and detection, so a symlinked hooks directory could not be uninstalled
past -- RemoveGitHook is the only uninstall path -- while

InstallGitHook and failing every agent turn on the same refusal. Split
hooksRoot into ForInstall (refuses) and ForRemoval (resolves), and point
removal and detection at the latter: both act only on files Entire wrote,
so following the link costs nothing the install-time refusal protected.

A hook that could not be READ was classified "not foreign", so it got no

the target at all. An unreadable hook was silently destroyed where the
in-place write it replaced failed loudly with EACCES. classifyExistingHook
now identifies absent/ours/foreign positively and refuses to write on
anything else; removal treats the same case as present-and-not-ours so a
backup is not renamed over it either.
